failure_summary.description: The answer identified the right entity or category but differed from the expected concise name or grammatical form.
The answer selected a related place, work, or example instead of the target explicitly requested by the clue.
A fragment naming multiple places was treated as a travel topic rather than a cue to their shared attribute.

patch.reasoning: Most target-selection and name-form errors are already addressed by the skill, so repeating those rules risks adding no value. Two narrow gaps remain: terse clues can cue an attribute shared by multiple places, and a corporate designator can be redundant when the clue already supplies the organization type.

edits.target: When choosing a name form, distinguish identity-bearing parts from generic type words supplied by the clue. Retain conventional initials that belong to a person's identifying name; omit a generic label such as an entity type or location type when the clue supplies that type and the shorter name identifies the answer unambiguously.
edits.content: For organizations, omit a legal or generic designator such as “Company,” “Inc.,” or “Ltd.” when the clue already identifies the entity type and the core trade name is unambiguous. Retain it when it distinguishes the entity or is an inseparable part of its conventional name.

edits.target: When a prompt consists only of a place name, do not simply repeat it. If context clearly identifies its jurisdiction or location, treat the prompt as an elliptical request for that place attribute and answer with the supported information. Do not infer a relation when context does not make one clear.
edits.content: When a terse clue names multiple places in a shared construction such as “in X and Y,” look for the shared attribute the clue is likely cueing, such as language, country, or region. Use the wording and reliable context to select the intended relation; do not default to an unrelated topic prominent in noisy search results, and do not guess if several relations are equally plausible.
